title: How to improve the site so a human can decide — findings about the site itself, not about football
rule: each finding names the observed defect, the change proposed, and the verification that would prove the change worked. No site file outside this namespace is edited by this session except the additive root-nav entry produced by the shared generator.

rows.finding: The review object is fragmented: a reviewer must open 18 namespaces to see one decision asked 19 ways
rows.observed: counted at commit b340a49 by engine/inventory.py, and re-computed on every refresh: 20 peer suggestion registers / 156 rows, 18 question registers / 184 rows, 23 flag registers / 176 rows, 12 requirement registers / 456 rows in 31 nfl* namespaces; the requirement rows collapse to 130 text clusters, 409 of them inside a duplicated cluster, the largest holding 68
rows.proposed_change: one canonical review surface (CD-01 A) plus a generated cross-register index in it; per-namespace pages stay as appendices and each gains a one-line pointer
rows.verify_by: the landing page shows a single 'queue: N open / M decided' counter that a build failure enforces
rows.cost: one edit per index + one generator change
rows.risk_if_skipped: session count becomes inversely proportional to clarity

rows.finding: Nothing on the site records that a decision was made, so every session re-litigates the same blockers
rows.observed: 23 flag registers with 176 rows; the same class of item (no official price source; no official depth source; capture cadence) recurs across many of them with different ids and no cross-reference
rows.proposed_change: data/decisions.json, one row per suggestion id: verdict, decided_by, decided_utc, commit hash of the decision. The build refuses to publish 'recommended' text next to a decided row, so a decided item visibly leaves the queue
rows.verify_by: after one verdict is written, the counter moves and the row renders as decided
rows.cost: one file + ~15 lines of build logic
rows.risk_if_skipped: the suggestions section stays a reading list

sources.label: a peer register with the same empty-verdict design

rows.finding: Live tree counts and hard-coded dates share one sentence on the root nav, so the date goes stale while the number does not
rows.observed: the committed root index.html renders 'NFL research · 30 workspaces (2026-11-15)' where the count comes from a directory walk at build time and the date is a string literal in the generator
rows.proposed_change: move any 'as of' value into a data file the engine reads, and never render a date next to a computed count unless the date describes the count's own source commit
rows.verify_by: a test that fails when a rendered date does not appear in a data file
rows.risk_if_skipped: a reader trusts a stale date attached to a fresh number — exactly the class of defect this project flags elsewhere

sources.label: the generator line that computes the count

rows.finding: Flags are per-namespace, so an irregularity can be resolved in one place and still be open in another
rows.observed: 23 flag registers with 176 rows; the same class of item (no official price source; no official depth source; capture cadence) recurs across many of them with different ids and no cross-reference
rows.proposed_change: a generated cross-namespace flag index that clusters rows by text and shows, per cluster, which namespaces still carry it open; a row is closed by its own namespace only
rows.verify_by: cluster count is smaller than row count, and each cluster lists its members
rows.cost: one engine here (already prototyped by the duplication clustering in pages/consolidation.html)
rows.risk_if_skipped: the reviewer spends effort re-approving what was approved once

rows.finding: A 'decision-readiness table' exists many times with different row counts, so 'requirements met' means different things on different pages
rows.observed: 11 requirement/readiness registers, 386 rows total, statuses counted per register: no shared id space, and ids such as R-01 collide across namespaces
rows.proposed_change: one requirement id authority (prefix by the register that defines it, or a single shared file the integration session owns) and one published readiness table built from it
rows.verify_by: a verifier check that no two registers define the same bare id with different text
rows.cost: schema discipline; the check is cheap to add
rows.risk_if_skipped: '29 of 69 met' and '44 of 73 met' both look like progress and cannot be compared

rows.finding: 'Blank — unverified' is a good convention, but nothing states how a blank could be filled
rows.observed: blanks are widespread and correct; the site rarely pairs one with a named acquisition route, so a reviewer cannot tell a hard absence from an unexplored one
rows.proposed_change: every blank gains a one-line 'how this becomes non-blank' with an owner, adopting the answer_grade + discovery column pair used in this namespace's question register
rows.verify_by: a build check that any blank cell sits in a row whose register carries a non-empty discovery field
rows.risk_if_skipped: blanks look like laziness or like finality, and both are wrong

sources.label: the register whose rows pair an answer grade with a discovery action

rows.finding: There is no 'what changed since the last session' view, though the brief asks for a weekly diff
rows.observed: registers change silently between merges; the only way to see it is to diff files by hand
rows.proposed_change: an engine step that diffs committed registers against their previous commit and renders added/removed/changed row ids per page, with the commit hash of the comparison pinned in the artefact
rows.verify_by: the diff page names both commits and its row count equals the changed ids
rows.risk_if_skipped: the site's growth is invisible, so review effort concentrates on new pages instead of changed numbers

sources.label: peer register asking for the same feature

rows.finding: A reader cannot tell which pages describe a label rather than a feature, which is how look-ahead leakage enters a site like this
rows.observed: the game book — the most cited 'official source' in peer registers — contains final statistics, so any table built from it is post-game; only one peer namespace states that property in its own text
rows.proposed_change: a two-value field on every dataset row: point_in_time ∈ {pre-kickoff, post-game}, rendered as a column on the table itself and enforced by the verifier for any dataset a model would read
rows.verify_by: datasets with a missing point_in_time fail the build
rows.risk_if_skipped: a backtest silently grades itself against information published after kickoff

sources.label: the artefact whose content proves the point

rows.finding: Every namespace claims a verification, but there is no page listing what was NOT verified
rows.observed: peer pages report 'all checks passed' without a companion list of checks that could not run (e.g. 11 of 14 game centres never opened)
rows.proposed_change: each verifier prints a 'skipped by design' block, and the site renders it beside the pass count
rows.verify_by: the block exists on every page and is non-empty when coverage is partial
rows.risk_if_skipped: 'verified' acquires a meaning the data does not support
